newsitem.title: CROATIA: Shakeup in Croat police after attack on Moslems.
newsitem.headline: Shakeup in Croat police after attack on Moslems.

text.p: Bosnian Croat authorities named a new Croat police commander in Mostar on Wednesday after suspending senior police officials over their involvement in a shooting attack on Moslem religious pilgrims.

Bosnia's fragile Moslem-Croat federation was dealt a heavy blow last month when police in the west sector of Mostar ruled by Croat ultra-nationalists opened fire on Moslems trying to visit a cemetery. One Moslem was shot dead and 21 were wounded.

Croat authorities and media at first flatly denied Croat responsibility for the bloodshed before bowing to a U.N. inquiry which released photographs of Croat police, in uniform or plainclothed, shooting at fleeing Moslems.

Croat gangsters implicated in long-running violence against Moslem inhabitants of the Mostar region, including the February 10 shooting, were arrested last week in nearby Croatia, which backs Bosnian Croats, after strong protests by Western envoys.

The interior ministry of Herzegovina-Neretva County, which includes ethnically divided Mostar, named Jadranko Lovric as the new chief of police in Croat-controlled west Mostar, the Croatian state news agency HINA said.

He replaced Marko Radic, who was suspended along with deputy police chief Ivan Hrkac and police officers Zeljko Planinic and Bozo Peric pending a local investigation into their role in the February 10 bloodshed, it said.
HINA quoted the cantonal interior ministry as saying the inquiry so far established "a suspicion that the top officials of the west Mostar police are responsible (for the events)".

International peace coordinators are concerned that there have been no apparent moves to arrest Croat policemen who were photographed firing on the Moslem pilgrims, including suspended deputy chief Hrkac who has gone missing.

The Mostar incident has touched off apparent retaliatory Moslem attacks on Croat Catholic churches and buildings in the federation. The most recent was a bomb blast that damaged a Sarajevo church on Tuesday.
Bosnian Moslem authorities suspended four policemen pending an investigation into the bombing of the church which they were supposed to have been guarding.

Croat paramilitary gangs dominating western Mostar have been accused by Western envoys of inculcating a miasma of fear in the southwestern city to prevent its reunification as required by the Dayton peace agreement.
The government of Croatia has failed to uphold promises to remove hardliners in Bosnian Croat-held territory who enjoy strong links to President Franjo Tudjman's ruling party.
